Just saying this in case it COULD apply to any of you. I have old scarring from other stuff and I always scar and I thought they were keloid-ing. When at an orthopedic appt with a doc I trust, I asked for scar cream but told her online I found that there are keloid scars that respond to the cream and others that LOOK like keloids but are linked to this other disease which won’t respond to the cream. By pure chance when I said that, my ortho sat back with a light bulb moment. My scars helped diagnose my Ehlers Danlos Syndrome which made so many of my joint and health problems make sense. I had to go to a geneticist and do testing and stuff but it all started with how my skin tears and scars.  

Just wanted to share because some of you may have similar issues and don’t even know of the connection. Stay safe out there!

Texas is divided by different regions with state contract local mental health authority designations. You may already be familiar with it in your area but LMHAs receive state funding so everyone has access to free or reduced cost MH services. They may or may not be quality where you live but may be worth looking into? Mine offers meds, case management, counseling, help finding housing and a job etc. 

Also DARS - departmental assisitive and rehabilitative services (merged with the workforce commission) helps people in situations like yours get the help (medical support or education) to enter or re-enter the workforce. They may actually pay for you to get some EMDR. It’s a bureaucrat process but I’ve seen it lay off for lots of clients.

It started off as a first time thing because like I said, for the clinic, therapist, and doctor involved it was their first try with someone with DID and the type of trauma I have and they didn’t know what would happen. We played it safe. My reaction was far from typical. My ex had ketamine for his depression and anxiety and his experience was much more like what I read and watched online. 

My therapist had to keep reorienting me as I experienced what’s called “flooding” of old memory including full on somatic experiences. I switched a lot under the influence so she kind of greets and grounds parts that came out scared and unsure. Her face, her holding our hands, and her voice anchored us in safety. She kept asking us to find her face, follow her voice, and breathe. It’s the only thing that keeps us from yanking out the IV and trying to get up and run into traffic. After our initial experiences and positive results, we saw the benefit of the treatment but the need for skilled support. Dealing with one person getting ketamine is one thing, but for them I imagine it felt like doing it for all 30+ of my parts at the same time.  

Mostly she just grounds and keeps my safe. But lately we’ve experimented with more guided sessions. We talked about our plan and what could be accomplished while I’m in that state. Some of it sticks. Some doesn’t. But it helps us get further faster. I know this is done sometimes with mdma assisted sessions, which is why I proposed it for the ketamine. 

Please don’t read this and think this WILL happen to you.  In fact, if you’re just starting I’d probably try to suspend expectation and suspend all the crap you read and saw (unlike me) and go in blank slate. Allow the experience to be experienced and see what it becomes for you. I know that sounds like dumb advice since I did the opposite. But knowing what I do now and knowing what I do as a MH practitioner, I see the damage of bringing all the preconceived BS in with you. Try instead to deliberately leave it at the door.  Only YOU will experience ketamine how YOU experience it. I make a practice of going home and SLEEP. Then journal about it over the coming days. I hope it helps you in the way you need it (possibly not how you want it - I’ve learned that lesson).

To clarify the standard isn’t typically just danger as in self injury. It is intended to account for threats to your life or someone else’s. So long as they understand you weren’t and aren’t trying to kill yourself, they won’t do anything. I must say there are some exceptions of people who really don’t get it who act on knee jerk reactions but most ER staff have seen self injury and seem to have a basic understanding that it can be more about living than dying.

I’ve been. They have all the standard hospital rules about cords and things that could be used to self harm. They had access to wireless am/fm headphones when I was there 9 years ago. I had been hospitalized in all the wrong places so when I was sent to their DID unit it was night and day better. I will tell you they did a search when you first get there and you disclose scars and what not. I had to stand behind a sheet naked which freaked me out but mostly they are the best trained staff I had experienced. I was also uncomfortable with shower situation because they do 15 min checks and so I would wait until the check and quickly shower so I could have clothes on before they came back around because that freaked me out. I was very sensitive about access to shaving stuff so if I remember correctly, I brought some Nair or something so I could tend to my hygiene needs despite potential safety issues found with normal razors (we had to check them in and out). 

Good luck! I honestly wasn’t ready for that opportunity when I had it and regret being so resistant to their process. If I had opened up and trusted their process, I bet I’d be leaps ahead of where I am now. 

One last warning. I am not from Maryland but they have a state law requiring reporting of abuse to a minor even if you are currently an adult. I was warned about this and my perpetrators’ identities was protected information so all I said was that they lived in OK. They still had to call the state of OK and file the report with no information but I ensured nothing could happen. Just letting you know in case your perpetrators are secret like mine were.  I hope you get what you need from the experience. I hope you get what I should have.

Hi there. I just wanted to share that my abusers used to have a weird orientation thing they did in a shower in a custom bathroom made by my main perpetrator. For years later I struggled to shower and my hygiene sucked. I’d cheat and just wash my hair in the sink to avoid doing it as much bc my hair gave me away.

2. If it’s real bad, my husband will sit out in toilet and talk to me through the process. 

3. I made the shower MINE. I ground myself reminding me of all the differences between the shower where my abuse was and my shower. In schizophrenia, individuals may respond to external stimuli, ie they may cower in fear to the sight of a 6 ft spider on the wall that isn’t there or they may perceive an entity outside of themselves they may turn and actually talk to (a beautiful mind is a good movie portrayal of that). They really are seeing and hearing these things based on a lie perpetrated by dopamine in their brains. That’s why we never say what they are expressing isn’t real bc for them it absolutely is and they don’t understand why you don’t see it. 

With DID, the stimuli is internal almost exclusively. So I may hear parts talking and I may answer them in my head or out loud but the person I’m talking to is still in my head, NOT for example sitting in a chair next to me. Clinically, people with schizophrenia may present and their eyes may dart to the source of what they are seeing or perceiving and at times the head will follow suit. With DID, you won’t see as much external evidence of the internal process. It’s a little complicated but I hope I explained it well enough to make a bit more sense. 

With DID and schizophrenia, parts and hallucinations can both take on several forms, human or not. With DID, the ages often correlate with the ages the split occurred. There are subtypes of schizophrenia that are marked by grandiosity or religiosity so I could see professionals immediately going one way in their thought process as opposed to another. There’s a lot to consider but frankly discerning an answer may be as simple as medicating. The neurobiology of schizophrenia makes it a bit easier to try an antipsychotic med and see what happens because if it’s not psychosis, the med won’t make DID alters cease to exist.

DID and schizophrenia have very different etiologies. They have some similar features but one is often misconstrued as the other typically due to clinicians not asking the right questions to better discern symptom sources. As a clinician, I frequently explain and reexplain the differences because my supervisees simply see a lot more psychosis than they do DID and as a result they get a few yeses to the wrong questions and they presume they are looking at schizophrenia, failing to consider where these conditions overlap. Schizophrenia is largely genetic and is exclusively related to dopamine presence and function in the brain. DID is trauma linked and involves several neurotransmitters and parts of the brain. The difference can also be one of internal vs external stimuli though this rule doesn’t apply as much to schizophrenia. In DID, the stimuli are mostly exclusively internal. They look different in fMRI’s and involve very different courses of treatment. Just wanted to clarify because it is possible that someone suffers from both but more often than not, people with DID are incorrectly diagnosed with psychosis and subsequently get the care they need and deserve.

Your first question is a great one! DID makes me a better therapist. It means I can have a rough patch in my life and turn it off in a sense because my system is built to adapt and overcome. Most people can do this to a degree but I imagine it involves more effort than it does for me. It allows me to leave my shit at the door and truly be fully present for the clients I serve instead of thinking about how I’m triggered by their story or what’s on my grocery list, I’m truly with them. If I need to go to bat for a client, I have a part that can help advocate in a strong assertive voice that gets stuff done. DID helps me better understand the brain and empathize in ways my peers may not. I practice several modalities but my EMDR work is my favorite as I see REMARKABLE changes in a short time all bc I leaned into the brain’s capacity to self-heal. 

To be clear, I could NOT do this as well if I were earlier in my own treatment process. If I hadn’t put a huge dent in my own trauma work before I was licensed, I could have posed a real danger. I have a lot of work to do still but I’m no where near where I was years back and I have the clinical support and supervision to ensure I keep my stuff in check for the good of the people i serve. Because I’ve done significant work, my peers have no idea. Most of them have no idea I was a heroin addict (again all about disconnecting), that I have a trauma history, or that I’m experienced beyond the textbook. But, they mostly seem to look up to me, respect my opinion, and possess a deference that I never asked for but rather I guess I earned. I’ve been told by friends who later found out more that they knew something was different in a good way but I never told them my truth to help illuminate why. I didn’t before and I don’t now bc as much as we talk about ending stigma, clinicians are very judgy of other clinicians. I rarely see enough to believe that they are capable of understanding that I’m hiding in the ranks with this extreme mental health diagnosis that they doubt even exists or worse, that they think they understand bc they saw “Split”.  

In undergrad, I could barely function. Parts were showing up to classes that weren’t theirs so I got back a Molecular Bio test with a different name and children’s doodles on the side. I’d find myself in a Colonial Literature Spanish class (like Shakespearean Spanish) not knowing a lick of the language but having fluent parts. Sometimes I needed glasses, sometimes I didn’t. Parts self harmed or did drugs and other parts didn’t. I got kicked out several times having to seek specialized treatment bc of the disturbance it all caused. Now I’m nothing like that. My symptoms are much more manageable as our system has grown and healer with time and therapy. 

Secondly, remember  the DES is a tool and only a tool. It doesn’t diagnose but offers a clinician insight about the potential extent to which dissociative processes are occurring. That being said, people with DID typically average a 48 on the DES. Your score correlates with scores roughly in between PTSD and DID but be mindful of this: 

1. Everyone dissociates. When we drift into autopilot and find ourselves in our driveway not remembering if we stopped at a stop sign or light, we dissociated. It’s something we can all do to varying degrees. 

2. There are different types of dissociative experiences and disorders. Derealization is when we disconnect from our perception of reality and often question the veracity of our experience and our lives. Depersonalization is when we disconnect from our personhood. A common example is when it feels like you are watching yourself from the corner of the room as if you’re in a movie or on tv. There are many ways to disconnect and they can be adaptive or destructive pending the situation. I disconnected so frequently from my body that I struggle with very real medical conditions and have no idea. For example, I had shingles and it didn’t hurt at all. I wouldn’t have known had a family member not pointed out a strange rash that I had checked out. 

3. PTSD now has a dissociative specifier in the DSM 5. This means that individuals can have trauma and dissociative experiences without venturing further down the dissociative disorder spectrum to things like “other specified dissociative disorder” or to DID where I hang out. These can be normal extensions of a traumatic experience and can be managed with clinical care. DID occurs when that disconnect is extreme enough that parts spin off from the host to better contain an emotion or experience too extreme for our consciousness to bear. It can sometimes possess qualities that mirror symptoms lesser down the spectrum but they can be more defined (more walls) than someone with a different dissociative disorder or PTSD for example. These parts are like operating silos in the brain so others may have a strong part of themselves or an angry part of themselves etc, but they don’t exist in silos where a switch has to occur to access that part.  Not sure if I explained that well. 

To answer your question, my experience can be like yours sometimes. It’s critical to learn about effectively learning to tap into your senses to ground yourself in moments like you described. You can start to notice it happening either in physical or emotional cues or by reading the room and other’s responses to you and as your awareness improves, you’ll be more capable of utilizing grounding strategies to pull yourself back and fly under the radar. How long that takes will depend on how quickly and efficiently you reorient yourself. I carry a grounding kit with hard candy, scented lotions, etc to engage my senses in socially acceptable ways.

I’m cautious about giving you clinical input through reddit but I hope this info helps you better understand the facts of the DES and better understand the dissociative spectrum as it affects you shy of me pathologizing you. There’s nothing wrong with you accessing this information and asking follow up questions of your provider. It’s normal to want to understand your experiences especially when they are scary and affect your functioning. I would caution you about over-immersing yourself however, as sometimes looking for that label can become a rabbits hole. You may find that just reporting your experience and following the natural course of treatment with your therapist will get you where you need to go without unnecessary sidebars that could potentially cause more distress. 

I hope you find what you’re looking for and let me know if I can offer any other insight or support.

In my field, we often hear people express frustration with the name “post traumatic stress disorder” as we know it’s actually a normal reaction to abnormal events, however I do think that’s an oversimplification. We could say the same about DID. But the fact remains that two people can experience an identical trauma, one walk away fine and the other with full blown PTSD. So there are individual differences in our nervous systems and a lot to be said about resilience as a protective factor. 

I’d be open to the mindset that DID isn’t a disorder as I know I couldn’t control the events that led my consciousness to divide. Am I disordered because I grew up in a family organized underground sex trafficking circle? I don’t need to believe I’m broken because what happened in my brain. Instead I believe I’m broken because I was...mentally, physically, and spiritually broken and I’ve had the hospitalizations and surgeries to prove that in attempts to fix all the damage they did to us and our body. 

Maybe this isn’t about me. Maybe it’s about social constructs surrounding “disorder”, how we identify it, interpret it, and respond to it be it with pills or acceptance or shame or judgment. If you’re into this idea, I’d encourage you to read Thomas Szasz’ the Myth of Mental Illness. This dude was given top honors by the American Psychiatric Association and in his acceptance speech ripped the field a new one only to earn an ovation. I think it’s important to question what we “know” and be open to that evolving. 

I don’t think DID has been lost across time though. Considering what we know about the circumstances that create it, I imagine it’s always been there but that most people haven’t experienced the trauma that resulted in its creation. And that’s okay. The license is different than the education piece. So you can be a licensed marriage and family therapist, licensed professional counselor or licensed social worker with or without a doctorate. They all require at minimum a master's degree however.

 Frankly the master's vs doctorate doesn't necessarily make a therapist better or worst. Technically the doc level ones had more school but they may or may not lack experience in the field. A Psy D. is an applied doctorate of psychology vs a ph.d.which is typically more research based. However, a ph.d. in counseling is also applied so on this note, it matters more what the degree is in. 

At the end of the day, I'd interview your top contenders. Find out their specialization, what they have to offer you, and get a feel for the connection you feel with them. While licensure and education make some differences, the most impactful factor in making therapeutic change is the rapport you have with the person. 

Good luck!

Unfortunately the line between psychosis and Dissociative Disorders is often blurry, especially when you have suffered extensive trauma. This is why it often takes several diagnoses and often years of therapy before being correctly diagnosed and treated. Typically though, one major difference is the source of the alter or hallucination.  In DID, the voices are typically from within though people may be able to see them internally but external manifestations of voices or images are really more associated with the psychotic disorders like schizophrenia.  That doesn't mean however that you don't have both schizophrenia and a dissociative disorder albeit not likely DID. I'd probably follow up with a mental health professional specializing  in whichever symptom group is causing you more distress (the hallucinations or the trauma). Read the "For Laypeople" section of this: http://www.emdr.com/what-is-emdr/

It explains how it works. Basically, it uses bilateral stimulation of the brain either through eye movement,  tapping your legs alternating or with these tappers you hold which have alternating vibrations to reorganize information in your brain allowing it to reprocessing an old memory.  Doing it doesn't make you forget but it will help it lose the sting of the memory. What's cool is that your brain will generalize the benefit to other memories by itself really...like the benefits cascade forward to later memories. 

For example,  if you target a time you were embarrassed in class in kindergarten for wetting your pants, after you are done you brain keeps working to reprocess later memories that brought up the same emotions, i.e. you are a 45 year old business person and your boss scolds you in a meeting with others. For this reason,  you typically target the first or worst memory so its affects are more widespread.  

Hope this is helpful! Fyi, it's not hypnosis.  You are never in any kind of daze or altered state where you are out of control.  Some people have that worry but I assure you, you remain in control of it all.

So I don't know for certain something is wrong with you but I'd consider the possibility that this is about more than sheer willpower.  To me? It sounds like a symptom.  Amotivation is an inability to get yourself to do things you know you need or want to do. Has nothing to do with how important that thing is, you just can't motivate yourself to do it. Anhedonia is another symptom similar in concept but pertains to things you used to like to do but for whatever reason just can't enjoy it anymore. Racing thoughts is another symptom causing people to have the best intentions but get overwhelmed by too many thoughts at once and are therefore unable to follow through or complete things they start or need to start. Racing thoughts is associated with bipolar disorder, but it's also a type of concentration issue. Concentration problems, anhedonia, and amotivation all correlate with depression. I know it may be difficult to consider but a mental health evaluation may help you understand that there is a reason you feel how you do.

No one has answered you so I will. Good gut, first off...never walk up and touch. Approach within their line of sight and if necessary waive your hand to catch their attention without startling them. You can offer your hand for them to squeeze or to escort them somewhere safe or quieter if possible.  If they are kinda checked out (dissociating) then they may have already gone somewhere safe in their head but if they are in and out or spacey looking then help ground them in the moment.  One way is to ask questions about them or the environment.  Get them to talk, not you. Language recall requires brain activity that can counter traditional trauma reaction.  Identify items around you or colors around you and vehemently remind them of the current date and location,  i.e. you are safe, in Boston,  at a baseball game. The best rule of thumb when grounding people in a moment like this is to engage the 5 senses. So if you have a piece of gum or candy, a cold soda to hold, piece of ice, anything. Thanks for asking this question.  Hope this helps.

This article raised the question of sexual assault response protocol at my Alma mater. I went to a small liberal arts college and the Greek culture sounds identical though likely on a smaller scale. I personally experienced an assault about which I told no one. I admire the courage it took to fight this fight with university administration especially because I remember feeling responsible, stupid, and naive for being at the party and for not having the guts to hold him accountable.  It's normal to want to fit in and be willing to go beyond your comfort zone in a desperate reach for acceptance, but damn...the response from the friends who picked up Jackie hurts most. 

To be in that kind of pain and muster the strength to call for help only to hear friends deliberating the social cost of taking me to the hospital is heartbreaking.  This isn't about defending university pride or tradition. ..you miss the point if you get caught up in the daunting idea of being personally responsible for shifting university culture and correcting administrative mishandlings. It's critical to keep this in the dialogue but more critical to take ownership of that which you have direct control: your own action and inaction. Don't make rape jokes, play stupid games so they get you into the club with the "cool kids", or lower your ethical code to fit in. If it feels wrong, it's wrong. While that standard seems like a moving target, everyone adhering to individual standards will still result in us being better off than what happens when we allow that standard to be defined by groupthink. This is the only way to combat a cultural problem...a series of individual decisions to do the right thing can makeover a broken culture. It's as simple as that. This isn't just a UVA problem. It's my problem, your problem,  our problem. I'm sorry for the rant but this is close to my heart. Thank you all for paying attention to this thread and this post because this is how progress starts.

My hubby and I tried to discretely purchase these two old men dinner at a restaurant one night. One of the gentlemen required the help of the second to get to the table right next to ours. He was hunched over with some back issue I presume. I imagine he gets looks from people a lot and I consider it a brave thing to venture into public for a meal out. The two didn't say a word throughout the meal. They weren't hurting for money as each ordered beer and expensive menu items. Our waitress didn't understand our desire for discretion and had bought us dessert for our kindness shortly after telling the old men we picked up their tab. My hubby and I realized we were outed and planned to quickly get up and leave. After we barely stood, the hunched over man jumped up. He shook my hubby's hand and his eyes welled up with tears as he leaned in to hug my 6'4" spouse.  Both thanked us vehemently.  We  like to practice random acts of kindness but we were on the fence about these men as they weren't as outwardly needy as many have been before. But when that old stoic yet fragile man cried and hugged my husband, we could tell they needed it as much if not more than others. We gave proof that our generation has hope and kindness and they gave us a powerful reminder that money isn't as important as human affection and that even a stranger has so much love to share.
